message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | Your Rights (Texas) | What It Means for You | |------|---------------------|-----------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in inspection report, and receipts for any repairs you pay for. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc.).
• Texas Property Code §92.001–92.006 covers “unlawful detainer” and habitability. | If something is broken, give written notice and allow a reasonable time for repair. | | **Repair & Maintenance** | • Landlord must repair major defects that affect habitability.
• If the landlord fails to repair, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or sue for damages. | Document all repair requests and keep copies of correspondence. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if stated in the lease and must be reasonable. | Keep records of all payments. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies.
• Notice must be in writing and specify the purpose. | If you receive a notice, verify it’s in writing and that the purpose is legitimate. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice (except emergencies).
• You have the right to privacy in your rented space. | If you suspect unlawful entry, document the incident. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a lease with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• Landlord must provide a valid reason for termination if it’s a “no‑cause” eviction. | Keep a copy of the lease and any notice you receive. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the Texas “unlawful detainer” procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice to pay rent or quit), file a lawsuit, and obtain a judgment.
• You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | Keep all notices and court documents. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control laws. | Rent can increase at the end of a lease term if the lease allows it. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord may require you to pay utilities unless otherwise specified.
• If utilities are included, they must be maintained. | Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • You may sublet or assign the lease only with landlord’s written consent (unless the lease prohibits it). | Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Insurance** | • Landlord is not required to provide renter’s insurance, but you may want it for personal property protection. | Consider purchasing renter’s insurance. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If your landlord violates your rights, you can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, the Texas Commission on Human Rights, or the local housing agency.
• You may also sue for damages or seek a court order to compel compliance. | Keep all documentation (photos, receipts, correspondence). | ### Quick Tips for Protecting Your Rights 1. **Read the Lease Carefully** – All obligations and rights are usually spelled out in the lease. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help protect you if disputes arise. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – For repairs, entry, or termination, the lease and Texas law specify how much notice is required. 4. **Respond Promptly** – If you receive a notice (e.g., rent‑due notice, entry notice), respond in writing and keep a copy. 5. **Seek Help Early** – If you suspect a violation, contact a local tenant‑rights group or legal aid organization before the situation escalates. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | File complaints about landlord violations. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | File discrimination complaints. | | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs** | Information on fair housing and tenant rights. | | **Local Legal Aid Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance for tenants. | | **National Tenant Rights Organization** | Guides, templates, and advocacy resources. | If you have a specific issue (e.g., a landlord refusing to make repairs, a dispute over a security deposit, or a notice of eviction), let me know and I can provide more targeted guidance or help draft a letter to your landlord.
